summary:
Since the 1960s, NASA has left hardware on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space that varies widely in purpose and current function: rovers that completed their missions, instruments still at work, and probes still traveling away from Earth. Yet the stories of this hardware, and the science it made possible, remain scattered across technical sources that rarely reach children.

Our project aims to turn this information into stories children understand, and those stories into a journey of discovery. As our solution, we built "Uzay Mirası". Children explore 13 spacecraft in a 3D Solar System, from the Apollo 11 laser reflector to Perseverance and the Voyagers in interstellar space. NumberOne, an astronaut cat from Van, Türkiye, tells each story in the first person: why it was sent, what it discovered and whether it still works today. Children reinforce what they learn through quizzes and collect stamps in their Space Passport. All content is based on real NASA data and images; the app works in Turkish and English, offline.

It matters because it carries the legacy of space exploration to the next generation of scientists and shows how science is built through international collaboration.
details:
Project Details

What does it do and how does it work?

CosmoBots is a project that aims to tell school-age children the story of the hardware NASA has left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space since the 1960s. To achieve this, we built an interactive learning app called Uzay Mirası (“Space Heritage”). Each child picks a name and an avatar and creates a password-protected profile. Our guide, NumberOne, an astronaut cat from Van, Türkiye, welcomes them with a short tour.

The app’s main screen shows a 3D Solar System with orbiting planets. Children see 13 spacecraft in their real locations: the Apollo 11 laser reflector and the Lunar Roving Vehicle; on Mars, Viking 1, Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity, InSight, Perseverance and Ingenuity; in deep space, Pioneer 10, Voyager 1, Voyager 2 and New Horizons.

When a child taps a spacecraft, NumberOne flies there and tells its story aloud in the first person. Each story covers why the spacecraft was sent, its most important discovery, a “Did you know?” fact, a real NASA photo and a link to the source. Then come three questions: multiple choice, true/false and identify-the-photo. When the quiz starts, the information is hidden, so careful listening is rewarded, not memorization. Depending on the number of correct answers, the child earns a bronze, silver or gold stamp in their Space Passport. Badges, ranks and a leaderboard encourage children to keep playing. With the “Time Machine,” children can change the year and see where each spacecraft was from 1969 to today.

What are the benefits?

  • It brings NASA’s scattered, technical information together in one place, as stories children can understand.
  • It clearly shows the different states of the hardware: missions completed, still operating, and still traveling away from Earth.
  • Gamification helps children remember what they learn.
  • It needs no internet connection; it works at school, at home or at an event booth.
  • It is available in Turkish and English, so it can be used both locally and internationally.
  • It requires no account and collects no personal data; everything stays on the device.

What is the intended impact?

The goal of CosmoBots is for every child who plays Uzay Mirası to be able to tell, in their own words, the story of at least one NASA spacecraft and the science it made possible. We want children to become curious about space exploration, to see that science is a long-term effort built through international collaboration, and to develop an interest in science and engineering. As a first step, we plan to pilot the app in schools in Van and measure its impact with short pre- and post-game quizzes and the number of stamps collected.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did we use?

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Uzay Mirası is a single file and needs no installation.
    • Narration: Web Speech API
    • Sound effects: Web Audio API
    • Profile and progress storage: localStorage
    • Offline use and add-to-home-screen: Service Worker and PWA
    • Passwords: protected with SHA-256
  • AI: We used the AI assistant Claude for coding, content drafting and design. We checked all content against NASA sources.

How creative is our project?

  • The robots tell their own stories: Instead of a technical encyclopedia, each spacecraft speaks in the first person, creating an emotional connection between the child and the spacecraft.
  • Local identity: NumberOne, the astronaut cat from Van, is the guide, the game piece and the storyteller. Its mouth moves as it speaks, and it says “Meow!” when a child answers correctly.
  • Space Passport: Every spacecraft is a stop on the journey, and every lesson learned earns a stamp.
  • Attention-focused quizzes: Hiding the information when the quiz starts measures real learning.
  • Time Machine: Shows how space exploration has developed from 1969 to today.
  • Our own 3D engine: It is lightweight, so it runs even on low-end phones.

What factors did our team consider?

  • Accuracy: Dates, discoveries and mission statuses are based on NASA sources, and every story includes a source link.
    • Two languages.
    • Adjustable voice speed and pitch.
    • A “Sound Check” screen that diagnoses sound problems on Android and shows how to fix them.
    • The same font and layout on phones and computers.
  • Privacy and security: No account, email or personal information is required. Profiles are password-protected.
  • Offline use: The app works fully offline to avoid connection problems at schools and events.
  • Motivation: Stamps, badges, ranks and a leaderboard encourage children to play again.
  • Sustainability: Adding new spacecraft, questions or languages is easy. As next steps for CosmoBots, we plan to add a classroom mode, ESA and TUA (Turkish Space Agency) missions, and live NASA data.
